research_rationale:
EO 9301 (February 9, 1943, Franklin D. Roosevelt; 8 FR 1825, issue of Thursday, February 11, 1943), read in full in the held Federal Register text, declares that "For the duration of the war" no plant or place of employment is deemed to make the most effective use of manpower if its minimum workweek is under 48 hours (section 1, inside the lead row of the machine inventory), directs agencies to require contractors to comply (2), authorizes the Chairman of the War Manpower Commission to interpret the order and issue policies, directives and regulations and to set a different workweek in particular cases (3), requires agencies to comply (4) and states that the order is not to supersede other hours or wage laws (5). EO 9607 (August 30, 1945), held Federal Register text, revokes it by number in one sentence. The phrase "For the duration of the war" is an own-terms condition; no held instrument or source fixes a legal end of the war before August 30, 1945, and EO 9607 revokes the order outright without reciting that it had lapsed, so the first end is the express revocation.

A later general rule is not shown to have ended any command. Searches of the held corpus for \"Executive Order 9301\" and for the minimum-workweek wording found EO 9607 (the revocation) and EO 9332 (Solid Fuels Administration), which cites EO 9301 in a list of orders and does not revoke or amend it. The contents table of the held Federal Register issue of August 21, 1945 (10 FR page 10166) lists a rescission of the War Manpower Commission's regulations on the minimum wartime workweek; that page is not held, so the rescission's date and text cannot be read. Obligations that contractors incurred under contracts made while EO 9301 and the War Manpower Commission's regulations were in force arise from those contracts and the regulations, not from a continuing command of the order, and no held source shows any continuing effect; that is a disclosed qualification, not a finding.
